Because Nike was. Nike built its golf clubs in a facility in Fort Worth and exited the equipment business in 2016, which released a building and a group of experienced club builders into the same city. Artisan Golf was founded by two former Nike craftsmen, Mike Taylor and John Hatfield, in February 2017 and works out of the former Nike golf club facility. P53s Christopher Griffin leases space at Leonard Golf Links, in the building Nike used, from Marty Leonard daughter of Marvin Leonard, who founded Colonial.

Artisan grinds and finishes every club in Fort Worth. Edel hand-finishes its putters in Austin. P53 forges in the Pacific Northwest but does all machining, grinding and finishing in Fort Worth. Piretti mills in the United States. Lamb Crafted machines in Plano. BestGrips states designed and made in Texas. Clint Orms engraves by hand in Texas. On the apparel side it is mostly design here, sewing elsewhere Criquet prints made in Peru on the Top-Shelf Players Shirt, and Sierra Madres All Square Skort is Peruvian cotton.

Mike Taylor and John Hatfield, both former Nike employees. Hatfield has given the exact date: February 17, 2017 was their last day on the Nike payroll, and on Monday February 20 they walked in the same door and started Artisan. Taylor was Nikes model maker for irons and wedges; Hatfield built putters. Wedges are ground by Taylor personally and can only be ordered after an in-person fitting in Fort Worth.

It depends what you want. For a shirt you will wear off the course, Criquets Players Shirt is the obvious first purchase and has been for sixteen years. For something you will keep, a Clint Orms sterling ball marker or a set of BestGrips leather grips will outlast most of your bag. For clubs, Artisan is the one you travel for but you have to go to Fort Worth to be fitted, so treat it as a trip rather than a transaction.

The Grassy Issue The Feed Brands Field Guide Events About Feed / Drops & Brands / Brand to Know BEAMS Golf Brand to Know BEAMS Golf beams.co.jp Harajuku, Tokyo Est. 2011 Fashion-first golf from Japans most legendary retailer In 1976, a guy named Etsuzo Shitara opened a 21.5 square meter shop in Harajuku called American Life Shop BEAMS. Styled like a UCLA dorm room, stocked with early Nike running sneakers and West Coast campus wear his partner bought on trips to California with enormous empty bags. Fifty years later, BEAMS operates 160 stores with 50 sub-labels and is considered, in Nigos words, the very pinnacle of Tokyo culture. In 2011, they turned that editorial eye to golf and created Japans first select-shop golf brand.

The man behind it is Satoshi Nishiwaki, who joined BEAMS as a part-timer in 1995 and had never played golf before directing the brand. That turned out to be the point. BEAMS Golf doesnt start from performance and add style. It starts from fashion identity and engineers performance into it. Three sub-labels cover the range: Orange Label for American-casual boldness, Purple Label for modernized tradition, and B.G.THREE for minimalist city-to-course crossover. In 2019, a 20-year-old rookie named Hinako Shibuno wore BEAMS Golf Orange Label to win the AIG Womens British Open her first tournament outside Japan. The polo sold out within hours. BEAMS issued a victory commemorative edition four days later.

The collaboration list reads like a whos-who of taste: Malbon Golf, Polo Ralph Lauren, BRIEFING, Hender Scheme, SON OF THE CHEESE, Nike Golf, Jones Sports Co . Fifteen collaborations deep with Ralph Lauren alone. The catch is getting it stateside BEAMS ships internationally through WorldShopping, Buyee handles proxy orders, and the occasional Malbon or FARFETCH drop crosses the Pacific. That barrier is part of the appeal. You wont see it at the local muni. Youll know who did their homework.

The Brick is milled in the USA from premium stainless and hand-finished in Austin; the E-T01 is machined from carbon steel, then hand-painted, polished and assembled in Austin. Artisan grinds and finishes every club in Fort Worth. Edel hand-finishes its putters in Austin. P53 forges in the Pacific Northwest but does all machining, grinding and finishing in Fort Worth. Piretti mills in the United States. Lamb Crafted machines in Plano. BestGrips states designed and made in Texas. Clint Orms engraves by hand in Texas. On the apparel side it is mostly design here, sewing elsewhere Criquet prints made in Peru on the Top-Shelf Players Shirt, and Sierra Madres All Square Skort is Peruvian cotton.

In Austin. Edels own product pages state it plainly: The Brick is precision-milled in the U.S.A. from premium stainless steel and hand-finished in Austin, Texas, and the E-T01 is machined in the U.S.A. from premium carbon steel then hand-painted and assembled in Austin. Their wording is that each head is individually painted, polished and built by their master craftsmen. The brand was founded by David Edel and is known for fitting putters the way most fitters approach irons.

Edel Golf Fine Milled Repair Tool $45 Milled rather than stamped, which is the meaningful line in this category: a milled tool starts as a solid billet and holds an edge on the prongs instead of rolling over. Edel scripts its name across the face and leaves the rest alone. Shop

Milled versus stamped. A stamped tool is cut and pressed from sheet; a milled one is machined from solid billet. Milled prongs hold their geometry and resist rolling over at the tip, which is what turns a cheap tool into a bent one. Edel mills, Kraken mills, Gamut casts in brass. The $20 pieces are stamped, and at that price that is a fair exchange.

For $19.99 the Frogger HOP! opens one-handed and lives on a bag clip. For a tool you will keep, the Edel Fine Milled at $45 is milled rather than stamped. If you want something hand-made, Seamus forges its single-prong Greenskeeper in Portland at $76.

The flip weight shifts mass to the heel or the toe depending on how you order it, which means two of these can sit differently behind the ball at the same spec. Shop

It also runs through a lot of drop-down menus. Only a handful of these makers do one-off work: Show Out and the other independent engravers, Artisan in Fort Worth, KYOEIs custom programme, and Anthony Taranto, whose wedges are not for sale. Grindworks, Fourteen, Bettinardi, Edel, New Level, Indi and Miura all label their wedges custom, and all of them mean built-to-order from a fixed set of options. ekorre-golf.name: Ekorre Golf
src: Ekorre Golf Alignment Sticks Three Stripes 2,400 kr about $255 Built the way a split-cane fly rod is built: six matched sections of Swedish ash glued into a hexagonal rod, which gives the stick what the maker calls a memory it flexes and returns straight rather than taking a set. Sebastian Mateu, a cabinetmaker who caddied in Chile as a boy, developed it as his thesis at Malmstens in Stockholm on the elasticity of wood, and makes them at his workshop in Sigtuna. Three painted stripes, 80 to 85 grams a stick, custom colours for 200 kr, and import duty outside the EU is yours. Shop

Ash. ScotSticks makes the case that ash was golfs original wood before hickory crossed from America, and cuts its sticks from it in Scotland. Ekorre goes further and laminates six strips of Swedish ash into a hexagon, the way a split-cane fishing rod is made, so the stick flexes and returns straight.

The details that differ. Length runs 42 to 45 inches; Hickory & Heath picked 43 so the sticks sit below the woods in the bag. Ends are either capped bronze at Scotch & Skins, brass at Hazy, tack caps at Beavertail, nail caps at BubbaWhips or bare and chamfered, as ScotSticks and Ekorre prefer. Almost everyone engraves, and about half will paint your colours to order.

The makers here select straight-grained hickory, ash or walnut and most seal it against moisture; Ekorre laminates six strips of ash into a hexagon specifically so the stick returns to straight after flexing. Wood will always move a little more than a fiberglass rod, which is why several shops advise keeping the sticks out of a wet bag.

BubbaWhips (builder), Hickory & Heath (colours, stripe design, engraving), Beavertail (custom design plus free names), Nor'easter (its main line is fully custom; the ACK-ley is the stock pair), Thwack (Pick Your Own Hickory Switch, $139), Out West (engraving) and Ekorre (custom colours and a name for a fee).

The Grassy Issue The Feed Brands Field Guide Events About The Feed Drops J.Lindeberg Brand to Know J.Lindeberg Drops & Brands 28 August 2026 23 pieces Stockholm J.Lindeberg is the brand that made golf clothing fit, and it did it by dressing one Swede in trousers nobody else would wear. The label was founded in Stockholm in 1996 by Johan Lindeberg , who had spent the first half of the nineties building Diesel first as its distributor in Sweden, later running the American business and who arrived in golf with a fashion marketer's read on a sport that had stopped caring how it looked. Thirty years on, that founding argument has been so completely absorbed that it is hard to remember it was ever an argument.

Which brings it to Viktor Hovland , who has worn the brand since 2019 and re-signed for three more years in January 2025. His collection is the honest picture of J.Lindeberg now: quieter than the archive, built on technical solids, brown and oxblood and navy, with one colour-blocked polo in it that remembers what this label used to be. Everything below comes from that line, plus the anniversary capsule and a handful of tees.

30 YEARS AND A COLOUR J.Lindeberg is thirty this year and has chosen to celebrate by reselling its own origin story, which is either shameless or exactly right. The capsule is built around one colour and one afternoon in Texas, and the pieces carry the anniversary marks quietly enough that you would have to know what you were looking at.

SIX FROM THE HOVLAND LINE Viktor Hovland has worn J.Lindeberg since 2019 and extended for three more years in January 2025, which makes his collection the clearest statement of what the brand actually wants to be now. It is quieter than the archive suggests. Most of these are plain technical solids, and the one that breaks pattern is the one to look at.

WHERE THE BRAND MADE ITS NAME Trousers are the reason anyone knows this label. The story golf tells about J.Lindeberg is a story about leg width about a Swede turning up on the range in something cut close when everyone else was swimming in pleated XXXL. The current line is more restrained than that history, but the shapes are still the sharpest part of the range.

OFF-COURSE, MOSTLY The brand runs a serious tee programme because roughly forty per cent of the business is now fashion rather than golf, and the tees are where those two halves meet. None of these read as golf clothing, which is the point J.Lindeberg has always argued the clothes should work before and after the round as well as during it.

THE REST OF THE KIT Both halves of the brand come through here. The sneakers are the fashion side reasoning about golf shoes, and the bags are the golf side reasoning about how much a person will pay for one. The staff bag is the most expensive object J.Lindeberg sells to a man who is not buying outerwear.

src: The Golfers Journal Quarterly ~$100/yr 124 pages a quarter, zero ads a rule the magazine has never broken. Long-form storytelling, course photography that gets printed like it matters, and cultural essays that assume you can read more than 400 words at a stretch. Every issue is built to live on a shelf, not in a recycling bin, and after a few of them the subscription stops feeling expensive. This is the gold standard for independent golf publishing, and everything else on this list exists in the space it opened. Visit The Golfers Journal LINKS Magazine Quarterly ~$26/yr Running out of Hilton Head since 1988, which makes it the elder statesman of this list. LINKS covers the intersection of golf travel, course architecture, and lifestyle for the destination golfer the reader planning a Bandon trip, not grinding a handicap. At about $26 a year it is also the cheapest print subscription here, and the photography alone covers the ticket. Visit LINKS Magazine Kingdom Magazine Quarterly 200+ Pages Co-founded with Arnold Palmer, which tells you the register it operates in. Kingdom runs past 200 pages an issue luxury travel, course design, gear, and culture, produced with the heft of a fashion quarterly. It is the magazine for the golfer whose reading happens on planes to places with caddies. Not subtle, but it never claimed to be. Visit Kingdom Catalogue 18 Annual 300 Pages Golfs first subscription art magazine, and still the only one really trying it: 300 pages a year of course photography treated as fine art, printed once annually and built to be collected rather than consumed. There is no news in it and nothing dates. If the coffee-table book is your favorite golf format, this is the standing order to place. Visit Catalogue 18 Golf Course Architecture Quarterly Global The global journal of golf design and development, published quarterly by Tudor Rose. New builds, renovations, routing philosophy, turf, and the business behind all of it written seriously enough that the architects themselves read it. If The Fried Egg is the fans architecture outlet, this is the trade paper, and eavesdropping on the trade is half the fun. Visit Golf Course Architecture Bunkered 10x/Year Glasgow Scotlands biggest golf title, running out of Glasgow since 1996 at ten issues a year. Bunkered is lively and opinionated in a way the glossy monthlies rarely risk it will pick a fight on an equipment ruling and put a scowling tour pro on the cover. It covers the game from a distinctly Scottish perspective, which means the golf itself is taken seriously and everything else slightly less so. Visit Bunkered Indie Coffee Table & Culture Depeche Golf From Europe 22/issue From Europe with love. Depeche treats golf as a lens on the world rather than a sport in a vacuum culture, arts, ecology, and politics move through every issue. Five issues deep and getting better each time, and the fifth came bundled with a special-edition Mogshade headcover, which tells you the company it keeps. The most intellectually ambitious title on this list. Visit Depeche Golf Fairways France La Culture Golf Le magazine de la culture golf. The French entry on this list, covering the game the way the French cover everything travel, style, courses, and tour golf treated as culture rather than content. Club-house essays, best-golfs rankings, and its own fairways Cup event. Proof the indie golf-culture wave speaks more languages than English. Visit Fairways GolfPunk Germany The Cult Revival The German revival of the cult UK title that made golf publishing irreverent in the 2000s. GolfPunks promise is that a golf magazine can be funny, loose, and competent at the same time comic-book cover art, travel features, and gear coverage that refuses to take itself seriously. The most fun anyone is having in European golf media. Visit GolfPunk The Links Diary Triannual Scotland 17 Words, photography, and film from Scottish fairways no swing tips, no product reviews, no exceptions. Fourteen issues in, The Links Diary has kept a quiet, literary register that reads closer to a journal entry than a magazine feature, published three times a year at 17. It is the title on this list most likely to make you book a ferry. Golf Out looks as good on a shelf as it reads on a couch, and it is sold through Soft Hands Club, which is exactly the right shop window for it. 18 an issue, and issues do not hang around. src: Australia In stock Eldrick $24.95 RIPIT is an Australian brand built on the idea that a grip can carry artwork, and founder Todd Watts spent three years getting a print to survive the moulding before he sold one. The Eldrick is a deep oxblood with a line drawing worked into the surface rather than laid on top of it, and every RIPIT carries an alignment mark at both ends. They release in limited art series the way an apparel label runs drops. Visit RIPIT Grips

What the independents sell splits two ways. RIPIT and Stick Grips work on the full-swing set and treat the grip as a surface to print on, in limited art series and monogram repeats. The other three work on the putter, where BestGrips wraps cowhide by hand the way grips were made before rubber won on price, Garsen builds a trapezoid nobody else tools up for, and Rosemark moulds a micro-texture that has won ten million dollars on tour.

The economics explain the shape of the field. A full set is thirteen grips, so a Stick set runs about a hundred and seventy-five dollars and a RIPIT set about three hundred and twenty-five. That is why so many of these brands lead with putter grips. A putter grip is a single purchase, an easy first buy, and the one club where a golfer will tolerate something that looks unusual.

Five are covered here. RIPIT out of Australia for printed art-series grips at $24.95 and Stick Grips at $13.49 for full-swing sets; BestGrips in Conroe, Texas for handmade leather at $35, Garsen for the trapezoid QUAD at $39.99, and Rosemark for tour-proven micro-texture at $35 on the putter side.

A full set is thirteen grips. At Stick's $13.49 that comes to about $175, and at RIPIT's $24.95 about $324. That arithmetic is why several small brands lead with putter grips instead, which are a single purchase.

It is a moulded or printed reference on the grip that shows you where the club face is pointing without looking down at it. RIPIT puts one at both ends of every grip, and Stick moulds in separate hand and club-face markers. It is a rules-legal aid as long as it does not indicate line of play once you are over the ball.

What the independents sell splits two ways. RIPIT and Stick Grips work on the full-swing set and treat the grip as a surface to print on, in limited art series and monogram repeats. The other three work on the putter, where BestGrips wraps cowhide by hand the way grips were made before rubber won on price, Garsen builds a trapezoid nobody else tools up for, and Rosemark moulds a micro-texture that has won ten million dollars on tour.

The economics explain the shape of the field. A full set is thirteen grips, so a Stick set runs about a hundred and seventy-five dollars and a RIPIT set about three hundred and twenty-five. That is why so many of these brands lead with putter grips. A putter grip is a single purchase, an easy first buy, and the one club where a golfer will tolerate something that looks unusual.

Five are covered here. RIPIT out of Australia for printed art-series grips at $24.95 and Stick Grips at $13.49 for full-swing sets; BestGrips in Conroe, Texas for handmade leather at $35, Garsen for the trapezoid QUAD at $39.99, and Rosemark for tour-proven micro-texture at $35 on the putter side.

A full set is thirteen grips. At Stick's $13.49 that comes to about $175, and at RIPIT's $24.95 about $324. That arithmetic is why several small brands lead with putter grips instead, which are a single purchase.

It is a moulded or printed reference on the grip that shows you where the club face is pointing without looking down at it. RIPIT puts one at both ends of every grip, and Stick moulds in separate hand and club-face markers. It is a rules-legal aid as long as it does not indicate line of play once you are over the ball.

Rosemark sells into more than twenty-five countries. RIPIT is Australian and ships internationally from there. BestGrips, Stick and Garsen are US-based, so check shipping on the product page before ordering from abroad.

The catalogue reaches from a MacKenzie sailcloth bag at $1,400 down to a paper fan at $14, and both read as the same company. It started as a group chat. A few college roommates were graduating in 2011 and wanted somewhere to keep talking about golf, so they named the thread after the course they had spent four years on. The chat became an annual trip, and the trip became an Instagram account that at one point had more followers than Golf Digest. Ian Gilley filed the LLC in 2017 and has described the sequence as a happy little accident.

Sugarloaf Social Club is a subsidiary of Pro Shop, Inc., the golf media company founded by Chad Mumm and Joe Purzycki that raised roughly $20 million from the PGA Tour and Powerhouse Capital. Pro Shop also owns Skratch and GolfWRX. Skratch discloses the shared ownership in its own coverage of the brand.

zaleas-golf.name: Zalea's Golf Co.
src: Zoe Walker-Faure, founder Zaleas Golf Co. Hand-sewn, Palm Desert Zaleas does not market to men at all. The homepage reads Headcovers Made for HER GAME and every description names a lady golfer, but the gingham and stripe patterns are neutral enough to sit on anyones bag. It started as a dorm-room Etsy shop and the covers are still cut by Zoes mother and sewn by her grandmother, with every print drawn by Zoe herself. Twice a year the scrap becomes one-off covers, at $70. Visit Zaleas Golf Co.
